title: Following Finland: The Profound Shift That Transformed My School And Could Fix America's
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Stinehart, a South Carolina teacher, argues that American schools have responded to struggle by tightening academic pressure, cutting recess and extending seat time, when Finland recovered by doing the reverse. He describes Finland's whole-child model, with unstructured play, frequent breaks, outdoor learning and little high-stakes testing. He then reports applying the same approach at his own rural, high-poverty school through an afterschool Play Club, longer recess, a second recess and a before-school playground. The school saw disciplinary referrals fall 76 percent and bus referrals fall 94 percent, with test scores rising for Play Club students and 100 percent positive parent feedback. The move is to treat play as a school-culture lever that drives behavior and engagement rather than a distraction from instruction. He closes by calling the American habit of overregulating children a producer of compliance rather than thoughtful learners.
points: Cutting recess and adding instructional time is the wrong response to struggling schools; Finland improved by prioritizing unstructured play and student well-being.
Stinehart's own school, with no extra funding, reports a 76 percent drop in office referrals and a 94 percent drop in bus referrals after adding Play Club and longer recess.
Play breaks (Finland gives fifteen minutes per forty-five of instruction) are presented as returning students to class more focused, motivated and creative.
Rigid hallway rules, scripted lessons and silent lunches are framed as overcontrol that breeds compliance rather than independence and critical thinking.
His policy list: treat recess as essential, make outdoor learning normal, reduce standardized testing and give students real autonomy.
quotes: For years, we have recognized that our schools are struggling. In response, we’ve doubled down on academic rigor - cutting recess, extending instructional time, and hammering as much content as possible into students' minds.

Finnish students spend nearly fifteen hours per week in unstructured play at school, compared to American students - many of whom are lucky to receive twenty minutes of recess a day, if it isn’t taken away for extra instruction or as a consequence for poor behavior. Despite this dramatically different approach, Finland’s students consistently outperform their American peers by every metric now.

I started by creating an afterschool Play Club, where students engaged in two hours of unstructured play without any adult direction, structured games, or intervention. We then made recess longer and added a second recess to the day.
Office referrals for disciplinary issues dropped by 76 percent. Bus referrals - often a measure of student conflict and frustration - fell by 94 percent.
The American education system operates under the flawed assumption that more academic pressure leads to better outcomes. Finland’s success proves otherwise.

This overregulation does not produce better learners - it produces compliance. If we want students who are thoughtful, engaged, and capable of critical thinking, we must give them opportunities to practice those skills in real, meaningful ways.
